title: The greatest is charity (1 Corinthians 13:13)
hookLine: faith, hope, charity remain, and the greatest is charity
tomorrow: you reach the top. now what?

lines: WHAT GOES IN THE LAST BOX?
cards: Moving out comes down to boxes. What goes in the car, what goes to a cousin, what goes to the curb. You find out fast what you actually need.

Paul does the same packing with the whole spiritual life, in the Douay-Rheims: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity." Three things make it into the last box.
And he ranks them. Faith carried the path, hope anchored it. So why does love win?

teach.b: Paul gives the reason a few verses earlier: "Charity never falleth away." Prophecies end, knowledge passes, but love doesn't. Catholic readers, following Thomas Aquinas, draw it out.
Faith is trusting what you can't yet see; one day, they say, it gives way to seeing. Hope reaches for what you don't yet have; one day it gives way to having.

teach.h: LOVE IS THE ONE THAT LASTS.
teach.b: Love doesn't give way to anything. It's the one thing you already do now that you'll still be doing then. That's why it's the greatest: it's the only one that comes all the way through.
And it doesn't stay a private virtue.

The Second Vatican Council, writing about people of every religion, began from one human family: all peoples share one origin, it said, because God made the whole human race to live on the face of the earth, and share one final goal, God himself.
Then it drew the conclusion: we can't truly call on God as Father of all while refusing to treat any person as a brother or sister.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Church's document on other religions begins from one human race, not from what divides it. That's charity at full width.
The greatest of these isn't greatest because it's loudest. It's greatest because it lasts, and because it leaves nobody outside.

how: Catholics often hear 1 Corinthians 13 at weddings and funerals; the Church teaches charity as the greatest of the three theological virtues and the form of all the others.

games.q: what does “the greatest is charity” mean?
o: giving to the poor matters more than believing
love outlasts faith and hope, and reaches everyone
being kind matters more than going to church

games.q: the last box — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says the three are equal
he ranks them: "but the greatest of these is charity."
Paul gives a reason love is greatest: it never falls away
"Charity never falleth away," while prophecy and knowledge pass.
the Council's document on other religions begins from what divides people
it begins from one human family: one origin and one final goal.

games.q: a new neighbor from a different religion moves in next door, and your family isn't sure how close to get. from today's lesson, what does charity at full width point to?
o: be polite, and save real friendship for people who share your faith.
treat them as family: one human race, one origin.
wait to see whether they reach out first.
games.why: the Second Vatican Council began from one human race and said we can't call on God as Father while refusing to treat anyone as a brother or sister.

practice: Find a photo of someone you love, or just bring their face to mind, and look at it for a while without hurrying. Let one loving thing you could do for them this week come into focus, as small or plain as it wants to be.
If you pray, you can hold them before God in silence; that's enough.

wordCard.voice: The greatest is charity. Of faith, hope and love, the one that never falls away, and leaves nobody outside.

orig.note: Latin: love, charity. the word in the Latin of 1 Corinthians 13:13: maior autem horum est caritas.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the greatest of these, because love is what you'll still be doing when you arrive. See you at the top.

sources.q: And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity.

sources.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.23 a.6; I-II q.67 a.3–6

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions
